claims.text: Melting onset and progression in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is triggered by surface-induced elemental segregation.
Unequal diffusion rates among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu produce localized composition fluctuations at nanoparticle surfaces during heating.
Surface composition fluctuations reduce local configurational entropy.
Reduced configurational entropy at the surface lowers the local melting barrier.
Surface regions with reduced configurational entropy nucleate premelting that subsequently spreads inward.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneous, solid, and uniformly distributed in elemental composition.
The room-temperature baseline is a uniform, single-phase, high-entropy FeNiCrCoCu solid solution.
Nanoparticles with higher surface-to-volume ratios will exhibit lower melting-onset temperatures.
Unpassivated nanoparticles will exhibit lower melting-onset temperatures than surface-passivated nanoparticles.
Surface compositional heterogeneities will become detectable before complete melting.
The progression from premelting to complete melting will correlate with the extent of surface segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles up to approximately 20 nm in diameter under inert conditions and controlled heating rates.
At larger particle sizes, alternative melting pathways or effects may dominate.
Under oxidizing conditions, alternative melting pathways or surface effects may dominate.
Impurities could contribute to the observed thermal behavior.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen can promote phase segregation during thermal aging of a high-entropy alloy.
High-entropy alloys are generally formed from five or more principal elements in near-equal proportions and derive high mixing entropy from this composition.
